opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you'll know it when the system stops needing you to babysit it. Right now, every model we train is essentially frozen the moment training ends. You deploy it, it goes out into the world, it runs into a million situations it's never seen before, and it learns absolutely nothing from any of them. Then a few months later we gather a pile of new data, run another enormous training job, and ship a new snapshot. That's not how any intelligent creature we know of actually works.

So the test, for me, is pretty practical. Can you put a system into a real environment, have it struggle with something, fail, try again, and get measurably better at that thing over days and weeks, without a human going in and curating a dataset and kicking off a new run? And just as important, can it do that without falling apart? The failure mode everyone knows about is catastrophic forgetting: you learn the new thing and quietly lose three old things. A real continually learning architecture has to accumulate skill the way people do, where getting good at one job generally makes you a bit better at adjacent ones rather than worse.

There are a few signals I'd look for. One is that the learning curve inside a deployment looks like a learning curve rather than a flat line. Another is stability: you can let it run for a long time and capabilities compound instead of drifting or degrading. And the third, which I think is the deepest one, is sample efficiency. Humans can pick up a new tool or a new codebase from a handful of experiences. If we get an architecture where a few hundred meaningful interactions move the needle the way a whole fine-tuning dataset does today, that's when I'd start believing we've got the real thing.

I'll also say that I don't think it'll be a single eureka moment where you run a benchmark and a light turns green. It'll probably look more like a period where the old way of doing things, train, freeze, deploy, retrain, just starts to feel obviously clumsy by comparison. When the people using it can't imagine going back to static models, that's probably the clearest sign.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first sign won't be a benchmark number. It'll be a feeling of not having to restart. Right now, the way we train models, you do this enormous run, you freeze it, and then the model lives in a kind of amber. Everything it learns after that point is either stuffed into context or bolted on through fine-tuning that somebody has to orchestrate from the outside. The model never really gets to own its own experience.

So the test I keep coming back to is pretty simple. You give the system a task on Monday, it struggles, it makes some mistakes, and on Friday it does the same class of task and it's just better. Not because we retrained it, not because we wrote a better prompt, but because the thing it went through on Monday actually changed it. And crucially, it got better at Monday's thing without getting worse at everything else it already knew. That second half is where most approaches die. Catastrophic forgetting is real, and it's not a small engineering nuisance, it's the central problem.

The other signal I'd look for is that the learning compounds in a way you didn't explicitly design. If I have to specify in advance what skills the system is allowed to pick up, that's not really continual learning, that's a very fancy curriculum. What I want is to be surprised. I want to look at what it's figured out after a few months in the world and go, huh, we never put that in. That's roughly how you'd evaluate a good new hire, right? Not by whether they ace the onboarding quiz but by whether six months later they're doing things nobody taught them.

And then there's the boring but honest answer, which is that I'll know because the economics change. If the model is really learning on the job, the cost of making it useful in a new domain should fall off a cliff over time instead of staying flat. Right now every new vertical is basically a new project. When it starts to feel like the system is doing most of that adaptation work itself, and we're just supervising, that's when I'll believe we've actually found it rather than just approximated it.

I'll say one more thing. I don't think there's going to be a single moment where the architecture is "found." I think it's more likely we get something that works a little, we ship it, it teaches us what's wrong with it, and the iterations get shorter. Which is kind of fitting. The architecture for continual learning probably gets discovered continually.

astra-6.text:
I think the test is whether the system gets better from doing the work. You give it a task it can’t solve, you help it understand what went wrong, and then you give it a different task that requires the same underlying lesson. Does it succeed without you having to explain it again? And can it keep doing that without forgetting what it already knew?

A longer context window can make something look like learning, so I’d want to see that improvement persist beyond the particular conversation. If it can accumulate experience, use that experience in new situations, and need less supervision over time, that would be a strong signal. I don’t think we’ll know from looking at the architecture alone. We’ll know from watching how it changes as it works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real test is whether the system gets better from experience without us having to turn that experience into another training run. Can it encounter something it doesn’t know, learn how to handle it, and then use that knowledge the next time—even when the situation looks a little different?

And it has to do that without forgetting what it already knew. If every new capability comes at the expense of an old one, we haven’t solved the problem. I’d want to see that loop working over time: the system makes a mistake, gets feedback, and becomes reliably better. That would be much more convincing to me than a single benchmark result.
